\title{Metric Markov cotype two of $\ell_1$ with $C^2=3024$: a machine-checked proof}
\date{}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
For every stationary reversible Markov chain on $n$ states and every $x_1,\dots,x_n\in\ell_1$, there are $y_1,\dots,y_n\in\ell_1$ satisfying the metric Markov cotype two inequality with constant $C^2=3024$. Equivalently, $N_2(\ell_1)\le 12\sqrt{21}$. The argument has three ingredients: the cut representation of finitely many points of $\ell_1$, a cubic "flattening" map with a quartic potential, and a comparison between the geometric (resolvent) average and the Ces\`aro average of the transition matrices. The formal proof follows this outline in Lean 4 with Mathlib. It replaces the stopped martingale of the informal proof by deterministic resolvent identities and a telescoping summation. The final theorem keeps the reversibility hypothesis, but uses it only to derive stationarity.
\end{abstract}

\section{Statement}

Let $\ell_1$ be the real Banach space of real sequences $x=(x(k))_{k\ge1}$ with $\|x\|_1=\sum_{k\ge1}|x(k)|<\infty$. Write $\mathbb N=\{1,2,\ldots\}$ and $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$.

- A matrix $A=(a_{ij})_{i,j\in[n]}$ is \emph{stochastic} if its entries are nonnegative and every row sums to one.
- A \emph{probability vector} $\pi$ on $[n]$ has nonnegative entries summing to one; zero entries are allowed.
- $A$ is \emph{reversible} with respect to $\pi$ if $\pi_ia_{ij}=\pi_ja_{ji}$ for all $i,j$.
- $A^s$ denotes the $s$-th matrix power.

\begin{theorem}[Metric Markov cotype two of $\ell_1$; $C^2=3024$, i.e.\ $N_2(\ell_1)\le 12\sqrt{21}$]
Let $n,t\in\mathbb N$, let $\pi$ be a probability vector on $[n]$, and let $A$ be a stochastic matrix on $[n]$ that is reversible with respect to $\pi$. Then for all $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\ell_1$ there exist $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\ell_1$ such that
\[
 \sum_i\pi_i\|x_i-y_i\|_1^2
 +t\sum_{i,j}\pi_i a_{ij}\|y_i-y_j\|_1^2
 \le 3024\sum_{i,j}\pi_i
 \Bigl(\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^t A^s\Bigr)_{ij}\|x_i-x_j\|_1^2 .
\]
\end{theorem}

The informal proof uses reversibility only through stationarity, $\pi A=\pi$.

\section{Formalization}

The formalization is written in Lean 4 on top of Mathlib. The relevant Mathlib objects are:
- the space $\ell^p$ of $p$-summable sequences (\texttt{lp});
- real matrices indexed by $\Fin n=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ and their powers;
- unconditional sums of series (\texttt{tsum}).

\paragraph{Notation and conventions.}
- We write $\Fin n=\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ with its natural order. It replaces the source's $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$; the relabelling is immaterial.
- $\Pn$ is the (finite) set of all subsets of $\Fin n$, including $\emptyset$ and $\Fin n$.
- For a real sequence $(c_s)_{s\ge0}$ we write $\sum_{s\ge0}c_s$ for Lean's \texttt{tsum}. It is the sum of the series when the series is summable (for real series: absolutely convergent), and $0$ otherwise. In every statement below in which such a series occurs, it is summable under the stated hypotheses; where summability is part of a lemma's conclusion, this is said explicitly.
- For $t\in\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ we put
  \[p_t=\frac1{t+1},\qquad q_t=\frac t{t+1},\]
  so that $p_t+q_t=1$ and $0\le q_t<1$.
- $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker delta, and $\one{P}$ is $1$ if $P$ holds and $0$ otherwise.
- For a finite set $\iota$, weights $w:\iota\to\mathbb R$ and $u,v\in\mathbb R^\iota$ we use the abbreviations
  \[
  \nw{u}=\sum_{b}w_b|u_b|,\qquad \nh{u}^2=\sum_b w_bu_b^2,\qquad \ip uv=\sum_bw_bu_bv_b .
  \]
  These are pure notation; the weights are only assumed nonnegative.
- For a function $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $u\in\mathbb R^\iota$, $\Phi(u)\in\mathbb R^\iota$ is defined by $\Phi(u)_b=\varphi(u_b)$.

\paragraph{The space $\ell_1$.}
The space $\ell_1$ is Mathlib's $\ell^1$ space of real sequences indexed by $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$. Its norm is $\|f\|=\sum_{k\ge0}|f(k)|$ (\cref{lem:mc_L1_norm}). Shifting indices by one is a linear isometry onto the source's $\ell_1$ indexed by $\{1,2,\dots\}$, so nothing changes.

\PY{l+s+sd}{(indexed by ℕ; the shift from \PYZob{}1,2,...\PYZcb{} to \PYZob{}0,1,...\PYZcb{} is an isometry). }\PY{l+s+sd}{\PYZhy{}/}

\paragraph{Probability vectors.}
A vector $\pi:\Fin n\to\mathbb R$ is a probability vector if $\pi_i\ge0$ for all $i$ and $\sum_i\pi_i=1$.

\begin{Verbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\},breaklines=true]

\paragraph{Stochastic matrices.}
A real matrix $A$ indexed by $\Fin n\times\Fin n$ is stochastic if $A_{ij}\ge0$ for all $i,j$ and $\sum_jA_{ij}=1$ for every $i$.

\paragraph{Reversibility.}
$A$ is reversible with respect to $\pi$ if $\pi_iA_{ij}=\pi_jA_{ji}$ for all $i,j$. As a definition, this does not require $\pi$ to be a probability vector or $A$ to be stochastic.
\begin{leanblock}{Lean: \texttt{IsReversible}}

It is proved by the theorem \leanname{solution} (\cref{sec:final}). The statement reads as follows. Let $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and $t\in\mathbb N_0$ with $t\ge1$. Let $\pi:\Fin n\to\mathbb R$ be a probability vector, $A$ a stochastic matrix reversible with respect to $\pi$, and $x:\Fin n\to\ell_1$. Then there is $y:\Fin n\to\ell_1$ with
\[
\sum_{i}\pi_i\norm{x_i-y_i}^2+t\sum_{i}\sum_j\pi_iA_{ij}\norm{y_i-y_j}^2
\le 3024\sum_i\sum_j\pi_i\Bigl(\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tA^s_{ij}\Bigr)\norm{x_i-x_j}^2 .
\]
Here $A^s_{ij}$ denotes the $(i,j)$ entry of the matrix power $A^s$, and $t$ appears as a real number.

This is exactly the source statement, with the following remarks.
- The source's $t\in\mathbb N=\{1,2,\dots\}$ becomes $t\in\mathbb N_0$ with the hypothesis $t\ge1$.
- The case $n=0$ is allowed, but it is vacuous: there is no probability vector on the empty set.
- The source's closing remark (stationarity suffices) is not a separate formal theorem. Formally, reversibility enters only through \cref{lem:mc_stationary}. Every subsequent lemma assumes only the stationarity relation $\sum_i\pi_iA_{ij}=\pi_j$.

\section{Proof}

\subsection{Overview}

The formal proof builds the same points as the source: $y_i=T(\Phi(h_i))$, where $h_i=\sum_jG_{ij}z_j$ and
\[
G=\sum_{s\ge0}p_tq_t^sA^s
\]
is the resolvent. Indeed $h_i=p_t\sum_sq_t^s(A^sz)_i$ is the source's (eq.~resolvent). The steps correspond to the source as follows.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Preliminaries on $A$.}
\cref{lem:mc_stationary} derives stationarity from reversibility. \cref{lem:mc_pow_stochastic,lem:mc_pow_stationary} transfer stochasticity and stationarity to the powers $A^s$. \cref{lem:mc_resolvent_summable,lem:mc_resolvent_basic,lem:mc_resolvent_first_step_aux,lem:mc_resolvent_first_step} show that $G$ is a stationary stochastic matrix satisfying the first-step identities
\[
G=p_tI+q_tAG=p_tI+q_tGA .
\]
\cref{lem:mc_harmonic_point} is the source's (eq.~harmonic).

\item \emph{Finite cuts} (source Lemma~\ref{lem:cuts}).
The following lemmas build the cut representation. \cref{lem:mc_transfer} transfers a cube inequality back to $\ell_1$.
- \cref{lem:mc_cut_real_mono,lem:mc_cut_real_pointwise,lem:mc_cut_real} decompose one real coordinate into cuts.
- \cref{lem:mc_L1_norm,lem:mc_L1_of_bound,lem:mc_L1_affine_apply,lem:mc_L1_affine_contr,lem:mc_L1_dist_eq_aiprover_s0,lem:mc_L1_dist_eq} collect facts about $\ell_1$.
- \cref{lem:mc_cut_coords,lem:mc_cut_L1} assemble the cut representation.

\item \emph{Flat map} (source Lemma~\ref{lem:flat}).
\cref{lem:mc_phi_scalar,lem:mc_flat_increment} give the increment bound (eq.~increment) in the squared form $72\|a\|^2\|\delta\|^2+18\|\delta\|^4$. \cref{lem:mc_flat} is (eq.~flat). \cref{lem:mc_phi_vertex} says that $\Phi$ fixes binary vectors.

\item \emph{Martingale and stopped walk} (source Corollary~\ref{cor:martingale} and Section~\ref{sec:proof}).
This part is done without probability.
- \cref{lem:mc_one_step} is the conditional-expectation step: \cref{lem:mc_flat} averaged over one transition of the killed chain. The linear term cancels because of the mean-value relation $u=pv+q\sum_ka_kh_k$.
- \cref{lem:mc_cube_step} applies it with starting index $i_0$ (the source's $e=z_{X_0}$) and current index $j$. The killed transition goes to $z_j$ with weight $p_t$ and to $h_k$ with weight $q_tA_{jk}$.
- \cref{lem:mc_aggregate} replaces summation along the martingale. It multiplies these inequalities by $\pi_{i_0}G_{i_0j}$, which is $p_t$ times the expected occupation time of the alive state $j$ for a chain started at $i_0$. It then sums over $i_0,j$ and telescopes, using $\pi G=\pi$ and $G=p_tI+q_tGA$. The discarded nonnegative term $p_t\pi_i\nh{h_i-z_i}^4$ is the source's initial potential $\mathbb E\|M_0-e\|_H^4$.
- \cref{lem:mc_cube_energy_raw,lem:mc_cube_energy} conclude the cube inequality
  \[
  \sum_i\pi_i\nw{z_i-\Phi(h_i)}^2+t\sum_{i,j}\pi_iA_{ij}\nw{\Phi(h_i)-\Phi(h_j)}^2\le108\sum_{i,j}\pi_iG_{ij}\nh{z_i-z_j}^4 .
  \]
  The passage to the source's bound $B+tE_A\le108\sum\pi_iG_{ij}\|x_i-x_j\|_1^2$, in the source's notation $B$, $E_A$ of Section~\ref{sec:proof}, is made only in \cref{lem:mc_transfer}. It uses the cut distance identity $\norm{x_i-x_j}=\nw{z_i-z_j}$ of \cref{lem:mc_cut_L1} together with the bit identity $|\alpha-\beta|=(\alpha-\beta)^2$. The exact identity (eq.~jump-identity) of the source has no counterpart; only these inequalities are proved.
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Geometric versus Ces\`aro} (source Lemma~\ref{lem:comparison}). Put
\[
D(s)=\sum_{i,j}\pi_iA^s_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2 .
\]
The geometric endpoint cost is the series $\sum_sp_tq_t^sD(s)$ (\cref{lem:mc_resolvent_D_eq}).
- Subadditivity of $\sqrt D$ is \cref{lem:mc_D_subadd}. It uses \cref{lem:mc_triple_mul,lem:mc_triple_first,lem:mc_triple_second,lem:mc_weighted_tri}.
- The bound $D(t)\le4W$ is \cref{lem:mc_cesaro_Dt}.
- Instead of the random variables $J=\lfloor S/t\rfloor$ and $R=S-tJ$, the series is split termwise by Euclidean division $s=\lfloor s/t\rfloor t+(s\bmod t)$ (\cref{lem:mc_D_divmod,lem:mc_geom_cesaro_pre}).
- The bound $\mathbb EJ^2\le3$ becomes $\sum_sp_tq_t^s\lfloor s/t\rfloor^2\le3$. It is computed from the closed form of $\sum s^2q^s$ (\cref{lem:mc_hasSum_sq_geom,lem:mc_floor_div_sq_le,lem:mc_geom_sq_div}).
- The bound $\mathbb P(R=r)\le 2/t$ becomes the bound $2/t$ on the mass of each residue class, $\sum_{s\equiv r}p_tq_t^s$ (\cref{lem:mc_geom_mod_coeff_geom,lem:mc_geom_mod_coeff,lem:mc_geom_mod}).
- The pieces are combined in \cref{lem:mc_geom_cesaro,lem:mc_comparison}.

\paragraph{Further deviations from the source.}
- \emph{Cuts.} The formal cut representation is indexed by all subsets $B\subseteq\Fin n$, with weights $w_B\ge0$ that may vanish. It is produced by sorting each coordinate (\cref{lem:mc_cut_real_mono}), not by the explicit formula $(\min_B-\max_{B^c})_+$. There is no separate case "all points coincide".
- \emph{Integral bound.} The integral estimate in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:flat} is replaced by an explicit factorization of $\varphi(r')-\varphi(r)$.

\paragraph{Unused lemmas.}
The following are proved but not used by the final proof: \cref{lem:mc_harmonic_point,lem:mc_phi_scalar,lem:mc_minkowski,lem:mc_cesaro_blocks,lem:mc_geom_summable_bdd,lem:pow_stochastic}.

\subsection{Lemmas}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_stationary}]\label{lem:mc_stationary}
Let $\pi:\Fin n\to\mathbb R$ and let $A$ be a stochastic matrix that is reversible with respect to $\pi$. Then $\sum_i\pi_iA_{ij}=\pi_j$ for every $j\in\Fin n$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By reversibility, $\sum_i\pi_iA_{ij}=\sum_i\pi_jA_{ji}=\pi_j\sum_iA_{ji}$. The last sum is $1$ because $A$ is stochastic.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_pow_stochastic}]\label{lem:mc_pow_stochastic}
If $A$ is stochastic, then $A^s$ is stochastic for every $s\in\mathbb N_0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We use induction on $s$. The identity matrix is stochastic. Write $A^{s+1}=A^sA$. Its entries $\sum_kA^s_{ik}A_{kj}$ are sums of products of nonnegative numbers. Its row sums are
\[
\sum_j\sum_kA^s_{ik}A_{kj}=\sum_kA^s_{ik}\sum_jA_{kj}=\sum_kA^s_{ik}=1. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_pow_stationary}]\label{lem:mc_pow_stationary}
Let $\pi:\Fin n\to\mathbb R$ and let $A$ be a real matrix with $\sum_i\pi_iA_{ij}=\pi_j$ for all $j$. Then $\sum_i\pi_iA^s_{ij}=\pi_j$ for all $s\in\mathbb N_0$ and all $j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We use induction on $s$; the case $s=0$ is trivial. For the step, write $A^{s+1}=A^sA$ and interchange the finite sums:
\[
\sum_i\pi_i\sum_kA^s_{ik}A_{kj}=\sum_k\Bigl(\sum_i\pi_iA^s_{ik}\Bigr)A_{kj}=\sum_k\pi_kA_{kj}=\pi_j. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
By induction, using $A^{s+1}=AA^s$ together with nonnegativity and the row sums of $A$, one gets $0\le A^s_{ij}\le1$. The terms are therefore nonnegative and bounded by $p_tq_t^s$. The geometric series $\sum q_t^s$ converges because $0\le q_t<1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_resolvent_basic}]\label{lem:mc_resolvent_basic}
Let $t\in\mathbb N_0$ and $\pi:\Fin n\to\mathbb R$. Let $A$ be stochastic with $\sum_i\pi_iA_{ij}=\pi_j$ for all $j$. Let $G$ be the matrix with $G_{ij}=\sum_{s\ge0}p_tq_t^sA^s_{ij}$. Then:
- $G_{ij}\ge0$ for all $i,j$;
- $\sum_jG_{ij}=1$ for all $i$;
- $\sum_i\pi_iG_{ij}=\pi_j$ for all $j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Each series converges (\cref{lem:mc_resolvent_summable}). Since $A^s$ is stochastic (\cref{lem:mc_pow_stochastic}), each term is nonnegative, so $G_{ij}\ge0$.

The geometric series gives $\sum_sp_tq_t^s=p_t/(1-q_t)=1$. A finite sum of convergent series converges to the sum of the limits. Hence
\[
\sum_jG_{ij}=\sum_sp_tq_t^s\sum_jA^s_{ij}=\sum_sp_tq_t^s=1 .
\]
Likewise, by \cref{lem:mc_pow_stationary},
\[
\sum_i\pi_iG_{ij}=\sum_sp_tq_t^s\sum_i\pi_iA^s_{ij}=\pi_j\sum_sp_tq_t^s=\pi_j. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_resolvent_first_step_aux}]\label{lem:mc_resolvent_first_step_aux}
Let $p,q\in\mathbb R$ and let $A,G$ be real $\Fin n\times\Fin n$ matrices. Suppose that for all $i,j$ the series $\sum_sp\,q^sA^s_{ij}$ is summable and $G_{ij}=\sum_{s\ge0}p\,q^sA^s_{ij}$. Then for all $i,j$:
\[
G_{ij}=p\,\delta_{ij}+q\sum_kA_{ik}G_{kj}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
G_{ij}=p\,\delta_{ij}+q\sum_kG_{ik}A_{kj}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Exchanging the finite sum over $k$ with the convergent series and using $A^{s+1}=AA^s$ gives
\[
\sum_kA_{ik}G_{kj}=\sum_s\sum_kA_{ik}\,p\,q^sA^s_{kj}=\sum_sp\,q^sA^{s+1}_{ij}.
\]
Splitting off the term $s=0$ (where $A^0_{ij}=\delta_{ij}$) gives
\[
G_{ij}=p\,\delta_{ij}+\sum_sp\,q^{s+1}A^{s+1}_{ij}=p\,\delta_{ij}+q\sum_kA_{ik}G_{kj}.
\]
The second identity is proved the same way with $A^{s+1}=A^sA$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_resolvent_first_step}]\label{lem:mc_resolvent_first_step}
Let $t\in\mathbb N_0$, let $A$ be stochastic, and let $G_{ij}=\sum_{s\ge0}p_tq_t^sA^s_{ij}$. Then for all $i,j$:
\[
G_{ij}=p_t\delta_{ij}+q_t\sum_kA_{ik}G_{kj}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
G_{ij}=p_t\delta_{ij}+q_t\sum_kG_{ik}A_{kj}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_harmonic_point}]\label{lem:mc_harmonic_point}
Let $t\in\mathbb N_0$, let $\iota$ be any set, and let $A,G$ be real matrices. Assume:
- $G_{ij}\ge0$ and $\sum_jG_{ij}=1$;
- $G_{ij}=p_t\delta_{ij}+q_t\sum_kA_{ik}G_{kj}$ for all $i,j$;
- $z:\Fin n\to\mathbb R^\iota$ satisfies $z_i(b)\in\{0,1\}$ for all $i,b$.

Put $h_i(b)=\sum_jG_{ij}z_j(b)$. Then for all $i,b$:
\[
0\le h_i(b)\le1\qquad\text{and}\qquad h_i(b)=p_tz_i(b)+q_t\sum_kA_{ik}h_k(b).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The value $h_i(b)$ is a convex combination of numbers in $\{0,1\}$, since $G\ge0$ and the rows of $G$ sum to $1$. For the identity, substitute the first-step relation for $G_{ij}$. The $\delta$-term gives $p_tz_i(b)$. In the other term, exchange the sums over $j$ and $k$:
\[
\sum_j\Bigl(\sum_kA_{ik}G_{kj}\Bigr)z_j(b)=\sum_kA_{ik}h_k(b). \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_phi_scalar}]\label{lem:mc_phi_scalar}
Let $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $\varphi(r)=3r^2-2r^3$ for all $r$. Let $r,r'\in[0,1]$ and $d\in\{0,1\}$. Then
\[
|\varphi(r')-\varphi(r)|\le6|r-d|\,|r'-r|+3(r'-r)^2 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We have $\varphi(r')-\varphi(r)=(r'-r)K$ with
\[
K=3(r'+r)-2(r'^2+r'r+r^2).
\]
It suffices to show $|K|\le6|r-d|+3|r'-r|$. With $\delta=r'-r$ one has
\[
K=6r(1-r)+\delta(3-4r-2r').
\]
Here $|3-4r-2r'|\le3$ on $[0,1]^2$, and $0\le6r(1-r)\le6|r-d|$ for $d\in\{0,1\}$. The formal proof checks the bound on $K$ by a case analysis on $d$ and on the sign of $r'-r$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_flat_increment}]\label{lem:mc_flat_increment}
Let $\iota$ be finite, let $w:\iota\to\mathbb R$ with $w\ge0$, and let $\varphi(r)=3r^2-2r^3$ as in \cref{lem:mc_phi_scalar}. Let $u,u'\in[0,1]^\iota$ and $e\in\{0,1\}^\iota$. Then
\[
\nw{\Phi(u')-\Phi(u)}^2\le72\,\nh{u-e}^2\,\nh{u'-u}^2+18\,\nh{u'-u}^4 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Coordinatewise bound.} The factorization in \cref{lem:mc_phi_scalar} (reproved here) gives, for each $b$,
\[
|\varphi(u'_b)-\varphi(u_b)|\le6|u_b-e_b||u'_b-u_b|+3(u'_b-u_b)^2 .
\]

\emph{Summation.} Multiply by $w_b\ge0$ and sum. Writing $S=\sum_bw_b|u_b-e_b||u'_b-u_b|$, $B=\nh{u'-u}^2$ and $A=\nh{u-e}^2$, this gives
\[
\nw{\Phi(u')-\Phi(u)}\le6S+3B .
\]
The Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, applied to the vectors $(\sqrt{w_b}|u_b-e_b|)_b$ and $(\sqrt{w_b}|u'_b-u_b|)_b$, gives $S^2\le AB$.

\emph{Conclusion.} From $(6S-3B)^2\ge0$ we get $(6S+3B)^2\le72S^2+18B^2$. Since both sides are nonnegative,
\[
\nw{\Phi(u')-\Phi(u)}^2\le(6S+3B)^2\le72S^2+18B^2\le72AB+18B^2. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_flat}]\label{lem:mc_flat}
Under the hypotheses of \cref{lem:mc_flat_increment},
\[
\nw{\Phi(u')-\Phi(u)}^2\le108\Bigl(\nh{u'-e}^4-\nh{u-e}^4-4\nh{u-e}^2\ip{u-e}{u'-u}\Bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $S=\nh{u-e}^2$, $P=\nh{u'-u}^2$ and $I=\ip{u-e}{u'-u}$.

\emph{Exact identity.} Expanding the square gives $\nh{u'-e}^2=S+2I+P$. Hence the bracket equals
\[
R=(S+2I+P)^2-S^2-4SI=2SP+(2I+P)^2 .
\]

\emph{Comparison.} By \cref{lem:mc_flat_increment} it suffices to show $72SP+18P^2\le108R$. The Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives $I^2\le SP$. Therefore
\[
P^2\le2(2I+P)^2+8I^2\le2(2I+P)^2+8SP .
\]
Consequently
\[
72SP+18P^2\le216SP+36(2I+P)^2\le108R. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_one_step}]\label{lem:mc_one_step}
Let $\iota$ be finite, let $w\ge0$ on $\iota$, let $\varphi(r)=3r^2-2r^3$, and let $e\in\{0,1\}^\iota$. Let $p,q\ge0$ with $p+q=1$, and let $a:\Fin n\to\mathbb R$ with $a\ge0$ and $\sum_ka_k=1$. Let $u,v\in[0,1]^\iota$ and $h:\Fin n\to[0,1]^\iota$ satisfy
\[
u_b=p\,v_b+q\sum_ka_kh_k(b)\qquad\text{for all }b.
\]
Then
\[
p\,\nw{\Phi(v)-\Phi(u)}^2+q\sum_ka_k\nw{\Phi(h_k)-\Phi(u)}^2
\le108\Bigl(p\,\nh{v-e}^4+q\sum_ka_k\nh{h_k-e}^4-\nh{u-e}^4\Bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{lem:mc_flat} to the pairs $(u,v)$ and $(u,h_k)$. Multiply by $p$ and by $q\,a_k$ respectively, which are nonnegative, and sum.

\emph{Potential terms.} The terms $-\nh{u-e}^4$ add up to $-(p+q\sum_ka_k)\nh{u-e}^4=-\nh{u-e}^4$.

\emph{Linear terms.} They add up to $-432\,\nh{u-e}^2$ times
\[
p\,\ip{u-e}{v-u}+q\sum_ka_k\ip{u-e}{h_k-u}
=\Bigl\langle u-e,\;p\,v+q\sum_ka_kh_k-(p+q\textstyle\sum_ka_k)u\Bigr\rangle_w .
\]
This vanishes by the mean-value relation together with $p+q=1$ and $\sum_ka_k=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_aggregate}]\label{lem:mc_aggregate}
Let $t\in\mathbb N_0$, let $\pi:\Fin n\to\mathbb R$ with $\pi\ge0$, and let $A,G$ be real matrices. Assume:
- $G\ge0$;
- $G_{ij}=p_t\delta_{ij}+q_t\sum_kG_{ik}A_{kj}$ for all $i,j$;
- $\sum_i\pi_iG_{ij}=\pi_j$ for all $j$.

Let $B:\Fin n\to\mathbb R$ and $E,F^z,F^h:\Fin n\times\Fin n\to\mathbb R$ with $F^h\ge0$. Suppose that for all $i_0,j$:
\[
p_tB_j+q_t\sum_kA_{jk}E_{jk}\le108\Bigl(p_tF^z_{i_0j}+q_t\sum_kA_{jk}F^h_{i_0k}-F^h_{i_0j}\Bigr).
\]
Then
\[
\sum_j\pi_jB_j+t\sum_j\sum_k\pi_jA_{jk}E_{jk}\le108\sum_i\sum_j\pi_iG_{ij}F^z_{ij}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Multiply the hypothesis for $(i,j)$ by $\pi_iG_{ij}\ge0$ and sum over $i,j$.

\emph{Left side.} Since $\sum_i\pi_iG_{ij}=\pi_j$, it becomes
\[
p_t\sum_j\pi_jB_j+q_t\sum_{j,k}\pi_jA_{jk}E_{jk}.
\]

\emph{Right side.} Fix $i$. By the column first-step identity,
\[
\sum_jG_{ij}\,q_t\sum_kA_{jk}F^h_{ik}=\sum_k\Bigl(q_t\sum_jG_{ij}A_{jk}\Bigr)F^h_{ik}
=\sum_kG_{ik}F^h_{ik}-p_tF^h_{ii}.
\]
This telescopes against $-\sum_jG_{ij}F^h_{ij}$, so the right side equals
\[
108\sum_i\pi_i\Bigl(p_t\sum_jG_{ij}F^z_{ij}-p_tF^h_{ii}\Bigr).
\]
Since $\pi_ip_tF^h_{ii}\ge0$, this is at most $108\,p_t\sum_{i,j}\pi_iG_{ij}F^z_{ij}$.

\emph{Conclusion.} Multiply the resulting inequality by $t+1$ and use $(t+1)p_t=1$ and $(t+1)q_t=t$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_phi_vertex}]\label{lem:mc_phi_vertex}
If $\varphi(r)=3r^2-2r^3$ for all $r$ and $d\in\{0,1\}$, then $\varphi(d)=d$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_cube_step}]\label{lem:mc_cube_step}
Let $t\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $A$ be stochastic. Let $\iota$ be finite, $w\ge0$ on $\iota$, and $z:\Fin n\to\{0,1\}^\iota$. Let $\varphi(r)=3r^2-2r^3$. Let $G$ satisfy
- $G\ge0$ and $\sum_jG_{ij}=1$;
- $G_{ij}=p_t\delta_{ij}+q_t\sum_kA_{ik}G_{kj}$.

Put $h_k=\sum_lG_{kl}z_l\in\mathbb R^\iota$. Then for all $i_0,j\in\Fin n$,
\[
p_t\nw{\Phi(z_j)-\Phi(h_j)}^2+q_t\sum_kA_{jk}\nw{\Phi(h_k)-\Phi(h_j)}^2
\le108\Bigl(p_t\nh{z_j-z_{i_0}}^4+q_t\sum_kA_{jk}\nh{h_k-z_{i_0}}^4-\nh{h_j-z_{i_0}}^4\Bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{lem:mc_one_step} with the following data:
- $e=z_{i_0}$, $p=p_t$, $q=q_t$ (so $p,q\ge0$ and $p+q=1$);
- $a=(A_{jk})_k$, a probability vector because $A$ is stochastic;
- $u=h_j$, $v=z_j$, and the family $(h_k)_k$.

The values of $h_k$ lie in $[0,1]$ because they are convex combinations of bits. The mean-value relation $h_j=p_tz_j+q_t\sum_kA_{jk}h_k$ follows from the first-step identity, exactly as in \cref{lem:mc_harmonic_point}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_cube_energy_raw}]\label{lem:mc_cube_energy_raw}
Let $t\in\mathbb N_0$, $\pi\ge0$, and let $A$ be stochastic. Let $\iota,w,z,\varphi$ be as in \cref{lem:mc_cube_step}. Let $G$ satisfy
- $G\ge0$ and $\sum_jG_{ij}=1$;
- both first-step identities $G_{ij}=p_t\delta_{ij}+q_t\sum_kA_{ik}G_{kj}=p_t\delta_{ij}+q_t\sum_kG_{ik}A_{kj}$;
- $\sum_i\pi_iG_{ij}=\pi_j$.

With $h_k=\sum_lG_{kl}z_l$,
\[
\sum_j\pi_j\nw{\Phi(z_j)-\Phi(h_j)}^2+t\sum_j\sum_k\pi_jA_{jk}\nw{\Phi(h_k)-\Phi(h_j)}^2
\le108\sum_i\sum_j\pi_iG_{ij}\nh{z_j-z_i}^4 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{lem:mc_aggregate} with
\[
B_j=\nw{\Phi(z_j)-\Phi(h_j)}^2,\quad E_{jk}=\nw{\Phi(h_k)-\Phi(h_j)}^2,\quad
F^z_{ij}=\nh{z_j-z_i}^4,\quad F^h_{ij}=\nh{h_j-z_i}^4\ge0 .
\]
The required step inequality is \cref{lem:mc_cube_step}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_cube_energy}]\label{lem:mc_cube_energy}
Let $\pi$ be a probability vector, and otherwise keep the hypotheses of \cref{lem:mc_cube_energy_raw}. Then
\[
\sum_i\pi_i\nw{z_i-\Phi(h_i)}^2+t\sum_i\sum_j\pi_iA_{ij}\nw{\Phi(h_i)-\Phi(h_j)}^2
\le108\sum_i\sum_j\pi_iG_{ij}\nh{z_i-z_j}^4 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
This is \cref{lem:mc_cube_energy_raw}, which only needs $\pi\ge0$, rewritten in three ways:
- $\Phi(z_i)=z_i$ by \cref{lem:mc_phi_vertex};
- $|\alpha-\beta|=|\beta-\alpha|$;
- $(\alpha-\beta)^2=(\beta-\alpha)^2$. \qedhere
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_cut_real_mono}]\label{lem:mc_cut_real_mono}
Let $a:\Fin n\to\mathbb R$ be monotone. Then there exist $c:\Fin n\to\Pn$, $\mathrm{gap}:\Fin n\to\mathbb R$ and $v_0\in\mathbb R$ with:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathrm{gap}_r\ge0$ for all $r$;
\item $\sum_r\mathrm{gap}_r\le2\sum_i|a_i|$;
\item $|v_0|\le\sum_i|a_i|$;
\item $a_i=v_0+\sum_r\one{i\in c_r}\mathrm{gap}_r$ for all $i$;
\item $|a_i-a_j|=\sum_r|\one{i\in c_r}-\one{j\in c_r}|\,\mathrm{gap}_r$ for all $i,j$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $n=0$, everything is empty. Otherwise take:
- $c_r=\{i:r<i\}$ (an upper cut);
- $\mathrm{gap}_r=a_{r+1}-a_r$ for $r+1<n$ and $\mathrm{gap}_{n-1}=0$;
- $v_0=a_0$.

By monotonicity, $\mathrm{gap}_r\ge0$. By induction on $m$, $\sum_{r<m}\mathrm{gap}_r=a_m-a_0$ for $m<n$, and $\sum_r\one{i\in c_r}\mathrm{gap}_r=\sum_{r<i}\mathrm{gap}_r$. This gives (iv).

For (ii), $\sum_r\mathrm{gap}_r=a_{n-1}-a_0\le|a_{n-1}|+|a_0|\le2\sum|a_i|$. Item (iii) is clear.

For (v), assume $i\le j$. Then
\[
|\one{i\in c_r}-\one{j\in c_r}|\mathrm{gap}_r=\one{r<j}\mathrm{gap}_r-\one{r<i}\mathrm{gap}_r,
\]
and the sum is $a_j-a_i=|a_i-a_j|$. The case $j\le i$ follows by symmetry.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_cut_real_pointwise}]\label{lem:mc_cut_real_pointwise}
The conclusion of \cref{lem:mc_cut_real_mono} holds for every $a:\Fin n\to\mathbb R$, without the monotonicity assumption.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Mathlib's \texttt{Tuple.sort} provides a permutation $\sigma$ of $\Fin n$ with $a\circ\sigma$ monotone. Apply \cref{lem:mc_cut_real_mono} to $a\circ\sigma$ and replace $c_r$ by $\{i:\sigma^{-1}(i)\in c_r\}$. Items (iv) and (v) follow by evaluating at $\sigma^{-1}(i)$ and $\sigma^{-1}(j)$. The sum $\sum_i|a_i|$ is invariant under $\sigma$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_cut_real}]\label{lem:mc_cut_real}
For every $n$ there are functions $g:\Pn\times\mathbb R^{\Fin n}\to\mathbb R$, written $(B,a)\mapsto g_B(a)$, and $v:\mathbb R^{\Fin n}\to\mathbb R$ such that for every $a\in\mathbb R^{\Fin n}$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $g_B(a)\ge0$ for every $B$;
\item $g_B(a)\le2\sum_i|a_i|$ for every $B$;
\item $|v(a)|\le\sum_i|a_i|$;
\item $a_i=v(a)+\sum_{B\in\Pn}\one{i\in B}g_B(a)$ for all $i$;
\item $|a_i-a_j|=\sum_{B\in\Pn}|\one{i\in B}-\one{j\in B}|\,g_B(a)$ for all $i,j$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For each $a$, choose $c^a,\mathrm{gap}^a,v_0^a$ as in \cref{lem:mc_cut_real_pointwise}. Set
\[
v(a)=v_0^a,\qquad g_B(a)=\sum_r\one{B=c^a_r}\,\mathrm{gap}^a_r .
\]
Then for every $f:\Pn\to\mathbb R$,
\[
\sum_Bf(B)g_B(a)=\sum_rf(c^a_r)\mathrm{gap}^a_r .
\]
Items (iv) and (v) follow from the corresponding items of \cref{lem:mc_cut_real_pointwise}. Item (i) is clear, and
\[
g_B(a)\le\sum_r\mathrm{gap}^a_r\le2\sum|a_i|. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_L1_norm}]\label{lem:mc_L1_norm}
For $f\in\ell_1$, the sequence $(|f(k)|)_k$ is summable and $\norm f=\sum_{k\ge0}|f(k)|$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_L1_of_bound}]\label{lem:mc_L1_of_bound}
Let $f,g:\mathbb N_0\to\mathbb R$ with $g$ summable and $|f(k)|\le g(k)$ for all $k$. Then there is $F\in\ell_1$ with $F(k)=f(k)$ for all $k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_L1_affine_apply}]\label{lem:mc_L1_affine_apply}
Let $\iota$ be finite, $V\in\ell_1$, $b:\iota\to\ell_1$, $u\in\mathbb R^\iota$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$. Then
\[
\Bigl(V+\sum_Bu_Bb_B\Bigr)(k)=V(k)+\sum_Bu_Bb_B(k).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_L1_affine_contr}]\label{lem:mc_L1_affine_contr}
With $\iota,V,b$ as in \cref{lem:mc_L1_affine_apply} and $u,u'\in\mathbb R^\iota$,
\[
\Bigl\|\Bigl(V+\sum_Bu_Bb_B\Bigr)-\Bigl(V+\sum_Bu'_Bb_B\Bigr)\Bigr\|\le\sum_B\norm{b_B}\,|u_B-u'_B| .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The difference is $\sum_B(u_B-u'_B)b_B$. Apply the triangle inequality and homogeneity of the norm.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_L1_dist_eq_aiprover_s0}]\label{lem:mc_L1_dist_eq_aiprover_s0}
Let $\iota$ be finite, $x:\Fin n\to\ell_1$, and $b:\iota\to\ell_1$ with $b_B(k)\ge0$ for all $B,k$. Let $z:\Fin n\to\mathbb R^\iota$ satisfy
\[
|x_i(k)-x_j(k)|=\sum_B|z_i(B)-z_j(B)|\,b_B(k)\qquad\text{for all }i,j,k.
\]
Then $\norm{x_i-x_j}=\sum_B\norm{b_B}\,|z_i(B)-z_j(B)|$ for all $i,j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{lem:mc_L1_norm} and the hypothesis,
\[
\norm{x_i-x_j}=\sum_k|x_i(k)-x_j(k)|=\sum_k\sum_B|z_i(B)-z_j(B)|\,b_B(k).
\]
Each series $\sum_kb_B(k)$ converges, since $b_B\in\ell_1$. So the finite sum over $B$ and the series over $k$ may be interchanged. Finally, $\sum_kb_B(k)=\sum_k|b_B(k)|=\norm{b_B}$ by nonnegativity.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_cut_coords}]\label{lem:mc_cut_coords}
Let $x:\Fin n\to\ell_1$. Then there exist $b:\Pn\to\ell_1$ and $V\in\ell_1$ such that for all $B,i,j,k$:
- $b_B(k)\ge0$;
- $x_i(k)=V(k)+\sum_B\one{i\in B}b_B(k)$;
- $|x_i(k)-x_j(k)|=\sum_B|\one{i\in B}-\one{j\in B}|\,b_B(k)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $g,v$ be as in \cref{lem:mc_cut_real} and write $a^{(k)}=(x_i(k))_{i}$. Define
\[
b_B(k)=g_B(a^{(k)}),\qquad V(k)=v(a^{(k)}).
\]
The sequence $k\mapsto\sum_i|x_i(k)|$ is summable, as a finite sum of summable sequences (\cref{lem:mc_L1_norm}). By \cref{lem:mc_cut_real}~(i)--(iii),
\[
|b_B(k)|\le2\sum_i|x_i(k)|\qquad\text{and}\qquad|V(k)|\le\sum_i|x_i(k)|.
\]
Hence $b_B,V\in\ell_1$ by \cref{lem:mc_L1_of_bound}. The three properties are items (i), (iv) and (v) of \cref{lem:mc_cut_real}, applied to $a^{(k)}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_cut_L1}]\label{lem:mc_cut_L1}
Let $x:\Fin n\to\ell_1$, and for $i\in\Fin n$ let $z_i\in\{0,1\}^{\Pn}$ be given by $z_i(B)=\one{i\in B}$. Then there exist $w:\Pn\to\mathbb R$ and $T:\mathbb R^{\Pn}\to\ell_1$ such that:
- $w_B\ge0$ for all $B$;
- $T(z_i)=x_i$ for all $i$;
- $\norm{x_i-x_j}=\nw{z_i-z_j}$ for all $i,j$;
- $\norm{T(u)-T(u')}\le\nw{u-u'}$ for all $u,u'\in\mathbb R^{\Pn}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Take $b,V$ from \cref{lem:mc_cut_coords} and set
\[
w_B=\norm{b_B},\qquad T(u)=V+\sum_Bu_Bb_B .
\]
- $T(z_i)=x_i$ coordinatewise, by \cref{lem:mc_L1_affine_apply}.
- The distance identity is \cref{lem:mc_L1_dist_eq}.
- The contraction property is \cref{lem:mc_L1_affine_contr}. \qedhere
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_transfer}]\label{lem:mc_transfer}
Let $t\in\mathbb N_0$, $\pi\ge0$, and let $A$ have nonnegative entries. Let $x:\Fin n\to\ell_1$, $\iota$ finite, $w\ge0$ on $\iota$, and $z:\Fin n\to\{0,1\}^\iota$. Let $T:\mathbb R^\iota\to\ell_1$ satisfy
- $T(z_i)=x_i$;
- $\norm{x_i-x_j}=\nw{z_i-z_j}$ for all $i,j$;
- $\norm{T(u)-T(u')}\le\nw{u-u'}$ for all $u,u'$.

Let $G$ be any real matrix and $c:\Fin n\to\mathbb R^\iota$ such that
\[
\sum_i\pi_i\nw{z_i-c_i}^2+t\sum_{i,j}\pi_iA_{ij}\nw{c_i-c_j}^2\le108\sum_{i,j}\pi_iG_{ij}\nh{z_i-z_j}^4 .
\]
Then there is $y:\Fin n\to\ell_1$ with
\[
\sum_i\pi_i\norm{x_i-y_i}^2+t\sum_{i,j}\pi_iA_{ij}\norm{y_i-y_j}^2\le108\sum_{i,j}\pi_iG_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2 .

\begin{proof}
Take $y_i=T(c_i)$. By the contraction property,
\[
\norm{x_i-y_i}=\norm{T(z_i)-T(c_i)}\le\nw{z_i-c_i}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\norm{y_i-y_j}\le\nw{c_i-c_j}.
\]
Square these, which is allowed since both sides are nonnegative. Multiply by $\pi_i\ge0$, resp.\ by $t\,\pi_iA_{ij}\ge0$, and sum; the left side is then bounded by the left side of the hypothesis.

For bits $\alpha,\beta$ we have $|\alpha-\beta|=(\alpha-\beta)^2$. Hence $\nh{z_i-z_j}^2=\nw{z_i-z_j}=\norm{x_i-x_j}$, and the right side of the hypothesis equals $108\sum\pi_iG_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_minkowski}]\label{lem:mc_minkowski}
Let $\alpha$ be finite, $\mu\ge0$ on $\alpha$, and $a,b\in\mathbb R^\alpha$. Then
\[
\Bigl(\sum_k\mu_k(a_k+b_k)^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\Bigl(\sum_k\mu_ka_k^2\Bigr)^{1/2}+\Bigl(\sum_k\mu_kb_k^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Apply Mathlib's Minkowski inequality \texttt{Real.Lp\_add\_le}, with exponent $2$, to the vectors $(\sqrt{\mu_k}a_k)_k$ and $(\sqrt{\mu_k}b_k)_k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_weighted_tri}]\label{lem:mc_weighted_tri}
Let $\alpha$ be finite, $\mu\ge0$ on $\alpha$, and $a,b,c\in\mathbb R^\alpha$ with $0\le c_k\le a_k+b_k$ for all $k$. Then
\[
\Bigl(\sum_k\mu_kc_k^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\Bigl(\sum_k\mu_ka_k^2\Bigr)^{1/2}+\Bigl(\sum_k\mu_kb_k^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $A,B$ denote the two roots on the right. Since $0\le c_k\le|a_k|+|b_k|$,
\[
\sum_k\mu_kc_k^2\le\sum_k\mu_k(|a_k|+|b_k|)^2=A^2+2\sum_k\mu_k|a_k||b_k|+B^2 .
\]
By Cauchy--Schwarz with the weights $\sqrt{\mu_k}$, $\sum_k\mu_k|a_k||b_k|\le AB$. Hence $\sum_k\mu_kc_k^2\le(A+B)^2$, and we take square roots, both sides being nonnegative.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_triple_mul}]\label{lem:mc_triple_mul}
For $\pi:\Fin n\to\mathbb R$, real matrices $P,Q$ and $d:\Fin n\times\Fin n\to\mathbb R$,
\[
\sum_i\sum_j\pi_i(PQ)_{ij}d_{ij}=\sum_{(i,k,j)\in\Fin n^3}\pi_iP_{ik}Q_{kj}d_{ij}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expand $(PQ)_{ij}=\sum_kP_{ik}Q_{kj}$, distribute, and reorder the finite sums.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_triple_first}]\label{lem:mc_triple_first}
If $\sum_jQ_{kj}=1$ for all $k$, then
\[
\sum_{(i,k,j)}\pi_iP_{ik}Q_{kj}d_{ik}=\sum_i\sum_k\pi_iP_{ik}d_{ik}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Sum over $i$ first and use $\sum_i\pi_iP_{ik}=\pi_k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_D_subadd}]\label{lem:mc_D_subadd}
Let $\pi$ be a probability vector and let $A$ be stochastic with $\sum_i\pi_iA_{ij}=\pi_j$ for all $j$. Let $x:\Fin n\to\ell_1$ and
\[
D(s)=\sum_i\sum_j\pi_iA^s_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2 .
\]
Then $\sqrt{D(r+s)}\le\sqrt{D(r)}+\sqrt{D(s)}$ for all $r,s\in\mathbb N_0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
On $\Fin n^3$ put $\mu(i,k,j)=\pi_iA^r_{ik}A^s_{kj}$; then $\mu\ge0$ by \cref{lem:mc_pow_stochastic}. We express the three quantities through $\mu$:
- Since $A^{r+s}=A^rA^s$, \cref{lem:mc_triple_mul} gives $D(r+s)=\sum\mu\,\norm{x_i-x_j}^2$.
- The rows of $A^s$ sum to $1$ (\cref{lem:mc_pow_stochastic}), so \cref{lem:mc_triple_first} gives $D(r)=\sum\mu\,\norm{x_i-x_k}^2$.
- $\pi A^r=\pi$ (\cref{lem:mc_pow_stationary}), so \cref{lem:mc_triple_second} gives $D(s)=\sum\mu\,\norm{x_k-x_j}^2$.

Finally, $\norm{x_i-x_j}\le\norm{x_i-x_k}+\norm{x_k-x_j}$. Apply \cref{lem:mc_weighted_tri}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_cesaro_Dt}]\label{lem:mc_cesaro_Dt}
Let $t\ge1$ and let $D:\mathbb N_0\to\mathbb R$ satisfy
- $D(0)=0$ and $D\ge0$;
- $\sqrt{D(r+s)}\le\sqrt{D(r)}+\sqrt{D(s)}$ for all $r,s$.

Then
\[
D(t)\le4\cdot\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tD(s).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $1\le r\le t$, subadditivity and $(\alpha+\beta)^2\le2\alpha^2+2\beta^2$ give
\[
D(t)\le2D(r)+2D(t-r).
\]
Summing over $r$ and reindexing $s=t-r$ (the term $r=t$ contributes $D(0)=0$) gives
\[
tD(t)\le2\sum_{r=1}^tD(r)+2\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}D(s)\le4\sum_{s=1}^tD(s),
\]
using $D\ge0$ in the last step. Divide by $t$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_cesaro_blocks}]\label{lem:mc_cesaro_blocks}
Let $t\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $D:\mathbb N_0\to\mathbb R$ with $D\ge0$ and $\sqrt D$ subadditive as above. Then for all $j,r\in\mathbb N_0$,
\[
D(jt+r)\le2j^2D(t)+2D(r).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By induction on $j$, $\sqrt{D(jt+r)}\le j\sqrt{D(t)}+\sqrt{D(r)}$. Square both sides and use $2\alpha\beta\le\alpha^2+\beta^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_hasSum_sq_geom}]\label{lem:mc_hasSum_sq_geom}
For $0\le r<1$, the series $\sum_{s\ge0}s^2r^s$ converges to $\dfrac{r(1+r)}{(1-r)^3}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $s^2=2\binom{s+2}{2}-3s-2$. Mathlib provides the sums
\[
\sum\tbinom{s+2}{2}r^s=(1-r)^{-3},\qquad\sum sr^s=r(1-r)^{-2},\qquad\sum r^s=(1-r)^{-1}.
\]
Hence the series converges to
\[
\frac{2}{(1-r)^3}-\frac{3r}{(1-r)^2}-\frac2{1-r}=\frac{r+r^2}{(1-r)^3}. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_floor_div_sq_le}]\label{lem:mc_floor_div_sq_le}
For $t\ge1$ and $s\in\mathbb N_0$, $\lfloor s/t\rfloor^2\le s^2/t^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We have $0\le\lfloor s/t\rfloor\le s/t$, because $\lfloor s/t\rfloor\,t\le s$. Square.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_geom_sq_div}]\label{lem:mc_geom_sq_div}
For $t\ge1$, the series $\sum_sp_tq_t^s\lfloor s/t\rfloor^2$ is summable and its sum is at most $3$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{lem:mc_floor_div_sq_le}, each term is between $0$ and $(p_t/t^2)s^2q_t^s$. By \cref{lem:mc_hasSum_sq_geom}, together with $1-q_t=p_t$, the dominating series has sum
\[
\frac{p_t}{t^2}\cdot\frac{q_t(1+q_t)}{p_t^3}=\frac{2t+1}{t}\le3. \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
\emph{A bound on $q_t^t$.} Bernoulli's inequality gives $(1+1/t)^t\ge2$. Since $q_t(1+1/t)=1$, it follows that $q_t^t\le1/2$.

\emph{Termwise bound.} Hence
\[
q_t^s=q_t^{s\bmod t}\,(q_t^t)^{\lfloor s/t\rfloor}\le2^{-\lfloor s/t\rfloor}.
\]

\emph{Reindexing.} On the residue class $\{s:s\bmod t=r\}$, the map $s\mapsto\lfloor s/t\rfloor$ is injective, and it maps $\{s<N\}$ into $\{k<N\}$. Therefore the sum is at most $p_t\sum_{k<N}2^{-k}\le2p_t\le2/t$, by \cref{lem:mc_geom_mod_coeff_geom}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_geom_mod}]\label{lem:mc_geom_mod}
Let $t\ge1$ and $f:\mathbb N_0\to\mathbb R$ with $f\ge0$. Then the series $\sum_sp_tq_t^sf(s\bmod t)$ is summable, and
\[
\sum_{s\ge0}p_tq_t^sf(s\bmod t)\le\frac2t\sum_{r=0}^{t-1}f(r).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Summability.} We have $f(s\bmod t)\le\sum_{r<t}f(r)$, so the series is dominated by a multiple of the geometric series.

\emph{Partial sums.} Split each partial sum over $s<N$ according to the residue $r=s\bmod t\in\{0,\dots,t-1\}$. On each class the factor $f(r)$ is constant, so by \cref{lem:mc_geom_mod_coeff} that class contributes at most $(2/t)f(r)$.

\emph{Conclusion.} A series of nonnegative terms whose partial sums are uniformly bounded has sum at most that bound.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_geom_summable_bdd}]\label{lem:mc_geom_summable_bdd}
Let $t\in\mathbb N_0$ and let $f:\mathbb N_0\to\mathbb R$ be nonnegative and bounded above. Then $\sum_sp_tq_t^sf(s)$ is summable.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Compare with $C\,p_tq_t^s$, where $C$ is an upper bound for $f$. For $t=0$ we have $q_0=0$, and the dominating series is trivially summable.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_D_divmod}]\label{lem:mc_D_divmod}
Let $t\in\mathbb N_0$ and $D\ge0$ with $\sqrt D$ subadditive. Then for all $s$,
\[
D(s)\le2\lfloor s/t\rfloor^2D(t)+2D(s\bmod t),
\]
with Lean's conventions $\lfloor s/0\rfloor=0$ and $s\bmod0=s$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $t=0$ the claim reads $D(s)\le2D(s)$. For $t\ge1$, write $s=jt+r$ with $j=\lfloor s/t\rfloor$ and $r=s\bmod t$.
- If $j=0$, then $D(s)=D(r)\le2D(r)$.
- If $j\ge1$, induction gives $\sqrt{D(jt)}\le j\sqrt{D(t)}$, so $D(jt)\le j^2D(t)$. Subadditivity gives $D(a+b)\le2D(a)+2D(b)$. Hence $D(s)\le2j^2D(t)+2D(r)$. \qedhere
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_geom_cesaro_pre}]\label{lem:mc_geom_cesaro_pre}
Let $t\ge1$, and let $D\ge0$ be bounded above with $\sqrt D$ subadditive. Then
\[
\sum_{s\ge0}p_tq_t^sD(s)\le2D(t)\sum_{s\ge0}p_tq_t^s\lfloor s/t\rfloor^2+2\sum_{s\ge0}p_tq_t^sD(s\bmod t).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
All three series are summable:
- the first and the third by boundedness of $D$ and comparison with the geometric series;
- the second because $\lfloor s/t\rfloor^2\le s^2$ and $\sum s^2q_t^s$ converges (Mathlib).

Multiply \cref{lem:mc_D_divmod} by $p_tq_t^s\ge0$, sum termwise, and split the right-hand series by linearity.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_range_le_Icc}]\label{lem:mc_range_le_Icc}
Let $t\in\mathbb N_0$, $D(0)=0$ and $D\ge0$. Then $\sum_{r=0}^{t-1}D(r)\le\sum_{s=1}^tD(s)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The two sums share the terms $1\le r\le t-1$. The left side has the extra term $D(0)=0$, and the right side has the extra term $D(t)\ge0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_geom_cesaro}]\label{lem:mc_geom_cesaro}
Let $t\ge1$ and let $D:\mathbb N_0\to\mathbb R$ satisfy
- $D(0)=0$, $D\ge0$ and $D$ bounded above;
- $\sqrt D$ subadditive.

Then
\[
\sum_{s\ge0}p_tq_t^sD(s)\le28\cdot\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tD(s).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $W=\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tD(s)$. Bound the two terms of \cref{lem:mc_geom_cesaro_pre}:
- By \cref{lem:mc_geom_sq_div} and then \cref{lem:mc_cesaro_Dt}, the first term is at most $2D(t)\cdot3\le24W$.
- By \cref{lem:mc_geom_mod} and then \cref{lem:mc_range_le_Icc}, the second term is at most $2\cdot\frac2t\sum_{r<t}D(r)\le4W$.

The total is at most $28W$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_resolvent_D_eq}]\label{lem:mc_resolvent_D_eq}
Let $t\in\mathbb N_0$, $\pi:\Fin n\to\mathbb R$, $A$ stochastic, and $x:\Fin n\to\ell_1$. Let $G_{ij}=\sum_sp_tq_t^sA^s_{ij}$ and $D(s)=\sum_{i,j}\pi_iA^s_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2$. Then
\[
\sum_i\sum_j\pi_iG_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2=\sum_{s\ge0}p_tq_t^sD(s).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Each series defining $G_{ij}$ converges (\cref{lem:mc_resolvent_summable}). Multiply it by the constant $\pi_i\norm{x_i-x_j}^2$. A finite sum over $(i,j)$ of convergent series converges to the sum of the limits. Its terms are $p_tq_t^sD(s)$. In particular, the proof shows that the series on the right converges; this is not part of the formal statement.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{pow_nonneg_entry}]\label{lem:pow_nonneg_entry}
If $A_{ij}\ge0$ for all $i,j$, then $A^s_{ij}\ge0$ for all $s,i,j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{pow_stochastic}]\label{lem:pow_stochastic}
If $A$ is stochastic, then $A^s$ is stochastic for every $s$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_D_props}]\label{lem:mc_D_props}
Let $\pi$ be a probability vector, $A$ stochastic, $x:\Fin n\to\ell_1$, and $D(s)=\sum_{i,j}\pi_iA^s_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2$. Then $D(0)=0$, $D(s)\ge0$ for all $s$, and $D$ is bounded above.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
- $A^0=I$, so $D(0)=\sum_i\pi_i\norm{x_i-x_i}^2=0$.
- Nonnegativity follows from \cref{lem:pow_nonneg_entry} and $\pi\ge0$.
- Since $0\le A^s_{ij}\le1$ (\cref{lem:pow_stochastic_entry_le_one}) and $0\le\pi_i\le1$, we get $D(s)\le\sum_{i,j}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2$. For $n=0$ the bound $0$ works. \qedhere
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_cesaro_rhs_eq}]\label{lem:mc_cesaro_rhs_eq}
For $t\in\mathbb N_0$, $\pi$, any real matrix $A$, $x:\Fin n\to\ell_1$ and $D$ as above,
\[
\sum_i\sum_j\pi_i\Bigl(\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tA^s_{ij}\Bigr)\norm{x_i-x_j}^2=\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tD(s).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Distribute, and interchange the finite sums over $i$, $j$ and $s$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{mc_comparison_aux}]\label{lem:mc_comparison_aux}
Let $t\ge1$, let $\pi$ be a probability vector, and let $A$ be stochastic with $\sum_i\pi_iA_{ij}=\pi_j$. Let $x:\Fin n\to\ell_1$, $G_{ij}=\sum_sp_tq_t^sA^s_{ij}$ and $D(s)=\sum_{i,j}\pi_iA^s_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2$. Then
\[
\sum_i\sum_j\pi_iG_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2\le28\sum_i\sum_j\pi_i\Bigl(\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tA^s_{ij}\Bigr)\norm{x_i-x_j}^2 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $n,t,\pi,A,x$ be as in the target statement, with $t\ge1$.

\emph{Step 1: stationarity.} By \cref{lem:mc_stationary}, $\sum_i\pi_iA_{ij}=\pi_j$ for all $j$. This is the only use of reversibility.

\emph{Step 2: cuts.} Put $z_i(B)=\one{i\in B}$ for $B\in\Pn$; these are bits. \cref{lem:mc_cut_L1} gives weights $w\ge0$ on $\Pn$ and a map $T:\mathbb R^{\Pn}\to\ell_1$ such that
- $T(z_i)=x_i$;
- $\norm{x_i-x_j}=\nw{z_i-z_j}$;
- $\norm{T(u)-T(u')}\le\nw{u-u'}$.

\emph{Step 3: resolvent.} Define $G_{ij}=\sum_{s\ge0}p_tq_t^sA^s_{ij}$. By \cref{lem:mc_resolvent_basic}, $G\ge0$, $G$ has row sums $1$, and $\sum_i\pi_iG_{ij}=\pi_j$. By \cref{lem:mc_resolvent_first_step}, $G=p_tI+q_tAG=p_tI+q_tGA$.

\emph{Step 4: cube inequality.} Let $\varphi(r)=3r^2-2r^3$ and $h_i=\sum_jG_{ij}z_j$. \cref{lem:mc_cube_energy}, with $\iota=\Pn$, gives
\[
\sum_i\pi_i\nw{z_i-\Phi(h_i)}^2+t\sum_{i,j}\pi_iA_{ij}\nw{\Phi(h_i)-\Phi(h_j)}^2\le108\sum_{i,j}\pi_iG_{ij}\nh{z_i-z_j}^4 .
\]

\emph{Step 5: transfer to $\ell_1$.} \cref{lem:mc_transfer}, with $c_i=\Phi(h_i)$ and using $\pi\ge0$ and $A\ge0$, produces $y_i=T(\Phi(h_i))\in\ell_1$ with
\[
\sum_i\pi_i\norm{x_i-y_i}^2+t\sum_{i,j}\pi_iA_{ij}\norm{y_i-y_j}^2\le108\sum_{i,j}\pi_iG_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2 .
\]

\emph{Step 6: comparison.} By \cref{lem:mc_comparison} (which uses $t\ge1$ and stationarity), the right side is at most
\[
108\cdot28\sum_{i,j}\pi_i\Bigl(\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tA^s_{ij}\Bigr)\norm{x_i-x_j}^2 .
\]
Since $108\cdot28=3024$, this is the asserted inequality.
\end{proof}

\section{Independent review}

A referee model (claude-opus-5-5), which took no part in the formalization or the proof, compared the verified Lean file with the source. Verdict: \textbf{FAITHFUL}.

\paragraph{Definitions.} \leanname{L1} is \leanname{lp} with constant fibre $\mathbb R$ over $\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}$ and exponent $1$. Its norm is $\sum_k |x(k)|$, which the proof confirms in \leanname{mc_L1_norm}. Re-indexing from $\{1,2,\ldots\}$ to $\{0,1,\ldots\}$ is an isometric isomorphism, so this is the source's $\ell_1$.

\leanname{IsProbVec} says the entries are nonnegative and sum to $1$; zero entries are allowed, as in the source.

\leanname{IsStochastic} says the entries are nonnegative and every row sums to $1$.

\leanname{IsReversible} is $\pi_i a_{ij}=\pi_j a_{ji}$ for all $i,j$, which is detailed balance as stated.

$A^s$ is the Mathlib monoid power on \leanname{Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) Real}, i.e. the ordinary matrix power.

No discrepancies.

\paragraph{Statement.} Quantification is over all $n,t\in\mathbb N$ with $1\le t$, every $\pi$ satisfying \leanname{IsProbVec}, every $A$ satisfying \leanname{IsStochastic} and \leanname{IsReversible}, and every family $x:\mathrm{Fin}\,n\to\ell_1$. This matches the source.

The case $n=0$ is admitted, but there the hypothesis $\sum_i\pi_i=1$ fails. That case is therefore vacuous, which is harmless because the source only concerns $n\ge1$.

The conclusion asserts the existence of $y$ with
\[\sum_i\pi_i\|x_i-y_i\|^2+t\sum_{i,j}\pi_i a_{ij}\|y_i-y_j\|^2\le 3024\sum_{i,j}\pi_i\Bigl(\tfrac1t\sum_{s\in[1,t]}(A^s)_{ij}\Bigr)\|x_i-x_j\|^2.\]
The range \leanname{Finset.Icc 1 t} is $\{1,\ldots,t\}$, and $1/t$ is well defined since $t\ge1$. This is exactly the source inequality with constant $3024$. Nothing extra needs to be supplied.

\paragraph{Proof.} \textbf{Cut representation (Lemma 1).} The cuts are built per coordinate.
\begin{itemize}
\item \leanname{mc_cut_real_mono} handles a sorted vector using upper cuts with gaps. \leanname{mc_cut_real_pointwise} reduces the general case to it via \leanname{Tuple.sort}.
\item \leanname{mc_cut_real} re-indexes the cuts by all subsets $B\subseteq[n]$, using choice. Zero weights and the empty and full sets are allowed; they are harmless.
\item \leanname{mc_cut_coords} and \leanname{mc_cut_L1} establish summability from the bounds $|v|\le\sum_i|x_i(k)|$ and $b_B\le2\sum_i|x_i(k)|$. They define $T(u)=V+\sum_B u_B b_B$ and prove $T(z_i)=x_i$, the distance identity, and the contraction property.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Resolvent.} \leanname{mc_resolvent_basic} and \leanname{mc_resolvent_first_step} define $G=p\sum_s q^sA^s$ and show it is stochastic and $\pi$-stationary. They also prove both first-step identities, $G=pI+qAG$ and $G=pI+qGA$. Stationarity of $\pi$ is derived from reversibility in \leanname{mc_stationary}, exactly as the source remarks.

\textbf{Flat map (Lemma 2).}
\begin{itemize}
\item \leanname{mc_flat_increment} proves the increment estimate (eq:increment) in squared form.
\item \leanname{mc_flat} proves (eq:flat) with constant $108$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Stopped walk (Corollary and Section 4).} This is the one place the formalization departs from the source. The martingale and stopping-time argument is replaced by a deterministic algebraic one.
\begin{itemize}
\item \leanname{mc_one_step} averages (eq:flat) over a single transition of the killed chain, with center $e=z_{i_0}$. The linear term cancels exactly by the harmonic identity.
\item \leanname{mc_aggregate} weights these one-step inequalities by $\pi_iG_{ij}$ and telescopes using $G=pI+qGA$. It then discards the nonnegative term $p\,F_h(i,i)$ and uses $\pi G=\pi$ on the left.
\end{itemize}
This is precisely the expectation over the stopped chain that the source computes, written as a Green's-function sum. It yields $B+tE_A\le108\sum_{i,j}\pi_iG_{ij}\|x_i-x_j\|_1^2$, i.e. the combination of (eq:stopped-bound) and (eq:jump-identity). \leanname{mc_transfer} then pushes this through $T$ using contractivity.

\textbf{Comparison (Lemma 3).} The structure follows the source closely; constants match ($E J^2\le3$, residue weight $\le2/t$, total $28$).
\begin{itemize}
\item \leanname{mc_resolvent_D_eq} rewrites the resolvent sum as $\sum_s pq^sD(s)$.
\item \leanname{mc_D_subadd} proves $L_2$ subadditivity, via Minkowski and stationarity.
\item \leanname{mc_cesaro_Dt} proves $D(t)\le4W$.
\item \leanname{mc_D_divmod} gives the block bound.
\item \leanname{mc_geom_sq_div} gives the bound $3$.
\item \leanname{mc_geom_mod} gives the $2/t$ residue weight.
\item \leanname{mc_range_le_Icc} uses $D(0)=0$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Conclusion.} The final step combines $108$ and $28$ by \leanname{linarith}, giving $3024$. No intermediate lemma is weaker than the step it represents.

\paragraph{Concerns.} None
